267.title: Not the jug (Avot 4:20)
267.hook: look not at the flask, but at what is inside it
267.howItsDone: Rabbi Meir's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder not to judge people or ideas by appearance, age or background.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gibor: the strong conquer their own urges, and the honored honor others. Your line was strong is self-mastered.

At a wine shop, there's a bottle with a gorgeous label, heavy glass, a wax seal. Next to it, a plain bottle with a label that looks like it was printed at home. The hand drifts toward the fancy one. Sometimes what's inside is thin and sour, and the plain bottle would've been wonderful. People get sorted the same way. The young intern, the older colleague, the guy with the accent, the woman in the wrong clothes. Near the end of chapter four, two sages argue about exactly this, using jugs of wine.
screen: `THE FANCY LABEL.` → `THE PLAIN BOTTLE.` → `TWO SAGES, AND JUGS OF WINE.`

segments.voice: One sage says: learning from the young is like eating unripe grapes and drinking wine straight from the press. Learning from the old is like eating ripe grapes and drinking aged wine. Experience matters, he's saying. Go to the elders. Then Rabbi Meir answers him. Don't look at the jug. Look at what's in it. There's a new jug full of old wine, and an old jug that doesn't even have new wine in it. A young person can hold deep, mature wisdom, and an old person can be empty. The container tells you nothing for sure. You have to taste. The Bible says something close to this when the prophet Samuel, choosing a king, is impressed by Jesse's tall eldest son, Eliab. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God tells him, "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." The chosen one turns out to be the youngest, out with the sheep. Rabbi Meir lived this. His own teacher, Elisha ben Abuyah, later left the path of the sages, and the others called him simply acher, the other one. The Talmud asks how Rabbi Meir could keep learning from him, and answers with a picture: he found a pomegranate, ate what was inside, and threw away the peel. That doesn't mean age and experience don't matter. It means you don't get to skip the tasting. Every person has to be met for what they actually hold.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've quietly sorted by their outside: too young to know anything, too old to get it, too loud, too plain, too different. Picture their face, set the label down, and wonder what's actually inside them, what they've lived through, what they might know. Stay curious for a few breaths.
Rabbi Meir, whose rule was: don't look at the container, look at what's in it. A new jug can hold old wine, and an old jug may hold none at all.

268.title: Four kinds of people (Avot 5:10)
268.hook: mine is mine and yours is yours; the saintly say mine is yours, the wicked say yours is mine
268.howItsDone: There is a custom of studying Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover, a chapter at a time, and its sayings are often discussed around the table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Meir: don't look at the jug, look at what's in it. Your line was you have to taste. Today, the last day in Pirkei Avot for now.

Roommates. One labels every yogurt in the fridge with a name and a date. One eats everything, whoever bought it. One quietly buys extra milk for the whole apartment and never mentions it. And one somehow always ends up with your charger, your hoodie and your leftovers, while his own stuff stays locked in his room. Chapter five of Pirkei Avot sorts people into four kinds, by one simple question: what do you say about mine and yours?
screen: `FOUR ROOMMATES.` → `LABELS ON THE YOGURT.` → `MINE AND YOURS.`

segments.voice: The one who says, what's mine is mine and what's yours is yours: that's the average person. Fair. Even. Nobody owes anybody. The one who says, what's mine is yours and what's yours is mine: the simple, unlearned person. Friendly, but with no sense of boundaries. The one who says, what's mine is yours, and what's yours is yours: the chasid, the saintly one, who gives freely and takes nothing. And the one who says, what's yours is mine and what's mine is mine: the wicked one. Now the surprise, hidden in the first type. The Mishnah adds: and some say, this is the way of Sodom. The perfectly fair one, like Sodom? The rabbis remembered Sodom not only for its violence but as a city where nobody shared, where, the prophet Ezekiel says, the poor and needy were never helped. Mine is mine and yours is yours can be fair. Taken all the way, it's a world where no one ever gives anything. So the saying pushes past fairness. What's mine is yours: that's the start of generosity, of giving without keeping score. And that closes these weeks in Pirkei Avot, sayings from a chain of teachers reaching back to Sinai. Judge slowly. Three legs to stand on. Open the door wide. Careful words. Pursue peace. Care for yourself, care beyond yourself. Crouch down anyway. Everything else grows from the heart. Ben chorin. Learn from everyone. And today, what's mine is yours. Tomorrow opens the much bigger conversation this little tractate belongs to.

269.title: What the Talmud is
269.hook: the Mishnah, gathered around 200 CE, and centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side
269.howItsDone: Many Jews study Talmud in pairs (chavruta), reading aloud and arguing through each passage, in yeshivas, synagogues, and study groups; some learn one page every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the chasid, who says what's mine is yours, and our last saying from Pirkei Avot for now. Your line was what's mine is yours. Today, a new part of the path.

Picture a page unlike any other. In the middle, a small block of text. Wrapped around it, on the inside edge, a column in a different typeface. On the outside edge, another. Around those, smaller notes, cross-references, tiny letters in the margins. It looks like a city seen from the air: an old town in the center, neighborhoods growing out in every direction. That's a page of Talmud. For the next few weeks, i'll give you a taste of it. And the first surprise: you've already been reading part of it.
screen: `A PAGE UNLIKE ANY OTHER.` → `A CITY FROM THE AIR.` → `A TASTE OF TALMUD.`

segments.voice: Start with the old town in the center. Remember Rabbi Judah the Prince, who taught that small commandments count? Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into one book, the Mishnah. It has six orders: farming and blessings, festivals, marriage and family, damages, holy things, and purity. Pirkei Avot, the sayings you just finished, is one small tractate of it. Then the rabbis kept talking. For the next few centuries, in the academies of the land of Israel and of Babylonia, they studied every line of the Mishnah and argued over it, in Hebrew and mostly in Aramaic. That discussion is the Gemara. Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud. There are two. The Jerusalem Talmud, from the land of Israel, and the larger Babylonian Talmud, the one most people mean. The word comes from the Hebrew root for learning and teaching. Here's what makes it unlike most holy books. It keeps the arguments. When two sages disagree, both opinions stay on the page, often with the losing side's reasons carefully preserved. Of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says: these and these are the words of the living God. And the page keeps growing. When it was printed in Venice in the fifteen-twenties, the layout put Rashi's commentary on the inner edge and the Tosafot, later scholars from France and Germany, on the outer. Later editions added more. One page, voices from many centuries, all talking at once.

270.title: There's no page one
270.hook: every tractate begins on page two, a reminder that no one starts at the true beginning
270.carry: nobody starts at the true beginning
270.howItsDone: Daf Yomi learners around the world study the same leaf of the Babylonian Talmud each day around the world, and each completed cycle is marked with a celebration called a siyum.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Talmud, the Mishnah at the center and voices from many centuries all around it. Your line was a conversation across centuries.

You've been meaning to start. Running, writing, an instrument, going back to school, the book you've always wanted to read. But you're waiting for the right beginning. A Monday. A new notebook. The first of the month. Everything cleared away so you can start clean, at page one. Here's something strange. Open any tractate of the Babylonian Talmud, in the standard printed editions, and look for page one. You won't find it. Every single one begins on page two.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE RIGHT BEGINNING.` → `A CLEAN PAGE ONE.` → `EVERY TRACTATE STARTS ON TWO.`

segments.voice: A page of Talmud is called a daf. Strictly, a daf is a leaf, with two sides: the front is side a, the back side b. So people cite the Talmud as, say, Berakhot two a: the tractate, the leaf, the side. Now, the missing page one. The usual practical explanation: when the Talmud was printed in Venice five hundred years ago, the first leaf of each volume was the title page. The text began on the next one, and every later edition kept the same numbering, so a page in one book matches a page in any other, anywhere in the world. But Jewish teachers found a lesson in it. There's no page one, they say, because no one ever starts at the true beginning. Before you opened this book, there was the Mishnah; before that, the oral teaching; before that, Sinai. You're always joining a conversation already underway. And a second lesson, often told in study halls: even when you've finished the whole Talmud, you still haven't mastered the first page. Learning never closes. Some learners built a whole practice around that idea. About a century ago, a rabbi named Meir Shapiro proposed that Jews everywhere learn the same daf each day, one leaf a day. It's called Daf Yomi. A cycle takes about seven and a half years, and when one ends, the celebrations fill arenas. Then, the next day, they start again. On page two.

271.title: The first question (Berakhot 2a)
271.hook: the whole Talmud opens by asking from when the evening Shema may be said
271.howItsDone: Observant Jews say the Shema in the evening prayer (Maariv) after nightfall and again at bedtime, and every Jewish day, including Shabbat and the holidays, begins at sundown.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the daf, and why every tractate starts on page two. Your line was nobody starts at the true beginning.

How would you open a book people would study for centuries? With God, maybe. With creation, or the meaning of life. The Talmud, the giant library of Jewish law and argument, opens with a question that sounds almost like a text to a friend. From what time can you say the evening Shema? That's the first line. No grand speech, no introduction. Just a practical question about tonight. And it turns out to hold a whole way of seeing time.
screen: `A BOOK FOR THE CENTURIES.` → `HOW DOES IT OPEN?` → `FROM WHAT TIME, TONIGHT?`

segments.voice: The Shema is the line at the heart of Jewish prayer, Hear, O Israel, said morning and evening. The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So the rabbis asked: lying down begins when, exactly? The Mishnah answers: from the time the priests go in to eat their holy food, at nightfall. And until when? Three answers. Rabbi Eliezer: until the end of the first watch of the night. The sages: until midnight. Rabban Gamliel: until the first light of dawn. Then a story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home late from a wedding feast, past midnight. We haven't said the Shema yet, they told him. He said: if dawn hasn't come, you still can, and you still should. Then the Talmud asks a question about the question. Why start with evening, and not morning? One answer: the verse itself says lying down first, then rising up. Another: in the story of creation, evening comes first. "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." That's the order the tradition follows. A Jewish day, Shabbat and every holiday begins in the evening, not at midnight or sunrise. The day starts in the dark and grows toward light. So the Talmud's first question isn't small at all. It asks you to notice the exact moment one day becomes the next, and to meet it with words.

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days: when does your evening really begin, when you close the laptop, when the kids are asleep, when the light outside changes color, when your phone finally goes face down? Picture meeting that moment on purpose, with one breath or one line you care about. If you pray, it could be the Shema; if not, it could simply be noticing: the day is turning.

272.title: On one foot (Shabbat 31a)
272.hook: a man asks Hillel for the whole Torah on one foot: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; go and learn
272.howItsDone: Hillel's answer is often taught to children, quoted in sermons, and paired with the Torah's command to love your neighbor as yourself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Talmud's very first question, about the evening Shema. Your line was when does evening start.

Give me the short version. Explain your job in one sentence. Sum up the whole book in a tweet. It's usually a little impatient, and a little unfair. Long ago, a man who wasn't Jewish walked up to Hillel, one of the great sages of his day, and made an impatient request. Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Everything. Before I lose my balance. Today, what Hillel said, and the line after it that often gets dropped.
screen: `GIVE ME THE SHORT VERSION.` → `THE WHOLE TORAH?` → `WHILE I STAND ON ONE FOOT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page 31a. The man says he'll convert if Hillel can teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel doesn't laugh or send him away. He accepts him, and says, in Aramaic: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is its commentary. Go and learn it. Three moves. First, the rule. It echoes the Torah's own words, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," from Leviticus. But Hillel turns it into something anyone can check. You may not always know what love asks of you. You almost always know what hurts. Start there. Second: the rest is commentary. Hillel doesn't say the rest doesn't matter. The Sabbath, the festivals, the food laws, the prayers: he calls all of it the explanation, that one rule worked out in real life. Third, the part people drop: go and learn. The summary fits on one foot. Living it takes both feet and the rest of your life. Hillel gives the man a door, not a shortcut. And notice who he says it to: an outsider, impatient, maybe a little rude. The whole Torah on one foot is also a lesson in how to answer a question like that.

273.title: Shammai's measuring stick (Shabbat 31a)
273.hook: the same man went first to Shammai, who pushed him away with a builder's rod
273.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often retell the stories of Hillel and Shammai together; the saying about being patient like Hillel is quoted to encourage kindness toward questioners and newcomers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hillel and the whole Torah on one foot. Your line was the rest is commentary.

Here's the part of yesterday's story that usually gets cut. Before the man ever reached Hillel, he knocked on another door: Shammai's, the other great sage of the generation. Same request. Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai had a builder's measuring rod in his hand. He pushed the man away with it. Only then did the man go to Hillel. So why does the Talmud bother to tell us?
screen: `FIRST HE KNOCKED ON SHAMMAI'S DOOR.` → `A BUILDER'S ROD IN HIS HAND.` → `PUSHED AWAY.`

segments.voice: The Talmud calls it the builder's cubit, a straight rod for measuring. It fits. Shammai measured things exactly, and a question that didn't measure up got pushed out the door. The same page tells two more stories like it. One man wants to accept only the written Torah, not the oral teaching. Another wants to convert so he can become high priest. Each time Shammai sends him away, and each time Hillel takes him in and teaches him patiently, until the man sees for himself. Right before these, the Talmud tells of a man who bet four hundred coins that he could make Hillel lose his temper. He knocked on Hillel's door on Friday afternoon, while Hillel was washing for Shabbat, and asked silly questions. Why are Babylonians' heads round? Hillel came out, answered kindly, and went back in. Again and again. The man lost his bet. So the Talmud draws a lesson: a person should always be humble and patient like Hillel, and not strict and impatient like Shammai. But Shammai isn't a villain. He was one of the great teachers, and his school's views are kept in the Mishnah beside Hillel's. His own famous saying, in Pirkei Avot: receive every person with a cheerful face. Maybe that was the lesson he taught himself. The measuring stick is real. So is the cheerful face.
screen: `THE BUILDER'S CUBIT.` · `THREE SEEKERS, TWO DOORS.` · `THE BET: MAKE HILLEL ANGRY.` · `SHAMMAI: A CHEERFUL FACE.` · then, large: `BE PATIENT LIKE HILLEL.`

segments.voice: This week ran from not judging the jug by its outside, through four kinds of people, what the Talmud is, page two and the first question, to the whole Torah on one foot. Now picture a question that tests your patience, a child's fifth why, a coworker asking the same thing again, and feel the rod in your hand. Then put it down, and answer the way Hillel did, kindly, one more time.
